title: The parts of a call
prompt: Click the part that tells R *what to do*.
hint:
Everything inside the brackets is material being handed over. Something
outside them decides what happens to it.

options.feedback:
Right. That's the function name — the job you're asking for.
Everything inside the brackets is material you're handing over for
it to work on.

This is the value being rounded, not the instruction. It's one of
the *arguments* — the things passed in to the function.

This is the second argument, saying how many decimal places you
want. Useful, but it isn't the part that decides what happens.

title: One argument instead of two
prompt:
You've been giving `round()` two arguments. What happens with only one?

```r
round(3.7)
```
hint: It doesn't fail, and it doesn't ask you to fill in the missing piece.

options.feedback:
Right. When you don't say how many decimal places you want,
`round()` uses zero. That value was always there, quietly doing its
job — you just never had to think about it. Most functions have
several of these, and some of them matter a great deal.

options.text: An error about a missing argument
options.feedback:
Some arguments are required and some aren't. The number of decimal
places has a fallback value that `round()` uses when you stay
silent.

options.text: `3.7` — with nothing to round to, it leaves the number alone
options.feedback:
It does round. The fallback isn't "do nothing", it's a specific
value: zero decimal places.

title: Reading the manual
prompt:
The help page for `round()` begins with this line, called *Usage*.

```r
round(x, digits = 0)
```

What is that line telling you?
hint:
One of the two arguments has something attached to it that the other
doesn't.

options.text: `x` must be supplied; `digits` will be 0 unless you say otherwise
options.feedback:
Exactly. An argument written with `= something` in the help page
has a fallback value, called a *default*. An argument written bare,
like `x`, has none — you have to supply it. This one line tells you
the name of every argument, the order they go in, and which ones
you can leave out.

The 0 is a starting point, not a rule. You've already overridden it
by writing `round(3.14159, 2)`.

options.text: It's an example of how someone might call the function
options.feedback:
It looks like an example, but it's a specification. The names are
the real argument names, in the real order, and the `= 0` shows
what happens if you say nothing.

title: Naming the arguments
prompt:
The usage line for `round()` showed that its two arguments are called `x`
and `digits`.
Fill in the names so the call says out loud what each number is for.
hint: Write the name, then `=`, then the value.

solution.why:
Naming an argument makes the code readable without the help page
open. In a long call with six or seven arguments, this is the
difference between code you can read at a glance and code you have to
take on trust.

checks.on_fail:
That didn't return 3.14. Check both names against the help line:
`round(x, digits = 0)`.

misconceptions.feedback:
Those are sensible descriptions, but R only accepts the actual
argument names. They're `x` and `digits`, exactly as the help page
spells them.

title: Does the order still matter?
prompt:
What does this return?

```r
round(digits = 2, x = 3.14159)
```
hint: Compare this with `round(2, 3.14159)` from the last module.

options.feedback:
Right. Once arguments are named, their position stops mattering —
R matches them by name instead. This is why you'll see named
arguments so often in generated code: the order becomes
unimportant, and anyone reading it can see what each value is for.

That would happen if R went by position, as it did in
`round(2, 3.7)`. The names override position entirely.

options.text: An error — arguments have to be in the right order
options.feedback:
Position only matters for arguments you haven't named. Name them
and you can write them in any order you like.

title: A default you didn't know about
prompt:
`log()` calculates a logarithm. What does this return?

```r
log(100)
```
hint:
The usage line for `log()` is `log(x, base = exp(1))`. That `exp(1)` is a
number
just under 2.72 — so whatever the default base is, it isn't 10.

options.feedback:
Right, and this is the one to remember. `log()` defaults to the
natural logarithm — base *e*, about 2.718 — not base 10. If you
wanted base 10 and didn't say so, you get an answer that is
perfectly correct, plausibly sized, and not the one you asked for.

That's `log10(100)`. It's a reasonable assumption, and it's wrong:
R's `log()` uses base *e* unless told otherwise. The number that
comes back, 4.61, is close enough to plausible that you might not
question it.

options.text: An error, because no base was given
options.feedback:
The base has a default, so the call runs. That's exactly what makes
it worth knowing about.

title: Overriding the default
prompt:
Make it a base-10 logarithm instead, so the answer comes back as 2.

The usage line for `log()` — which you'll also find in the **Functions**
panel — is `log(x, base = exp(1))`.
hint: You already know how to name an argument.

solution.why:
Supplying the argument replaces its default. `log(100, 10)` works too
— the second position is `base` — but naming it means nobody has to
remember that.

checks.on_fail:
The answer isn't 2. A base-10 logarithm asks: 10 raised to what
power gives 100? Check the number you passed as the base.

misconceptions.feedback:
`log10()` is a real function and it gives the right answer, so
that's a fine thing to reach for day to day. Here, though, the
exercise is about overriding a default — worth doing once with
`base =` so you can do it with any function, not just this one.

That's still the natural logarithm, so the base hasn't changed.
Check that a base is actually being passed in.

You've named the argument correctly — the problem is the number.
`base = 2` asks how many times you'd double 1 to reach 100. For a
base-10 logarithm the base is 10.

title: Rounding a half
prompt:
You're rounding tablet counts to whole numbers. What does R return here?

```r
round(0.5)
```
hint:
Try predicting `round(1.5)` as well. The pair together is more revealing
than either alone.

options.feedback:
Yes, and most people find this surprising. R rounds a half to the
nearest *even* number, so `round(0.5)` is 0 while `round(1.5)` is
2. It's a deliberate choice — over many values it avoids the upward
drift you'd get from always rounding up — and it's written in the
help page. But nobody reads the help page for `round()`, because
everybody already knows what rounding is. That's the shape of the
problem: the functions you'd never think to check are the ones
whose behaviour you're most likely to have assumed.

Worth knowing that this isn't R being odd. Python rounds halves the
same way; JavaScript rounds them up; Excel rounds them away from
zero. Four tools, three answers, all of them defensible.

That's the rule you were taught — halves go up. R doesn't do that.
It rounds to the nearest even number, so 0.5 becomes 0 and 1.5
becomes 2. Worth knowing before you round a dose.

R has a rule for it and applies the rule silently. The rule just
isn't the one most people expect.

title: Keeping what a function gives back
prompt:
A calculation has given you a dose of 3.7 tablets. A function hands
something back, and you can store it like any other value.

Round 3.7 to a whole number, store the result in `dose`, then double it.
hint: The whole call can go on the right of the arrow.

solution.why:
What a function returns is an ordinary value. You can store it, do
arithmetic on it, or pass it into another function — which is how
longer pipelines get built.

checks.on_fail: `dose` should hold 3.7 rounded to a whole number.
The second line should double whatever is in `dose`.

misconceptions.feedback:
That gets the right number, but you've done the rounding in your
head. Put the call itself on the right of the arrow — the point is
that a function's answer is a value you can keep.

title: A function you've never seen
prompt:
You've never met this function, and you don't need to. Click the named
argument.
hint: You're looking for a name, an equals sign, and a value.

options.feedback:
That's the function name. It sits outside the brackets, so it isn't
an argument at all.

This is an argument, but it's passed by position — no name attached
to it.

Also an argument, also unnamed. R works out what it's for from
where it sits.

Right. A name, an equals sign, a value. You still don't know what
`paste()` does, and you could already say: it takes some things,
and one of its arguments is called `sep`. That's usually enough to
ask a sharper question — or to notice that an argument you cared
about was never given a value at all.
